title: These Sunscreens Are Completely Undetectable on Deep Skin Tones - Allure

 Elegant formulas that use chemical filters and innovative ingredients to blend into deep skin tones seamlessly. By Tasha Nicole Smith November 18, 2026 Collage: Jemeria Davison; Source images: Courtesy of brands and editors Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Historically, sun-protection formulas weren't made with deeper tones in mind, leaving behind telltale white, gray, or purple casts. But today, the best sunscreens for dark skin blend seamlessly into the skin and dry down without a trace. Part of the reason is the advancement of chemical UV filters over the years. “Chemical sunscreens generally blend more invisibly,” says Maryland-based dermatologist Ife Rodney , MD. And thanks to even more recent innovations in sunscreen filters, like the long-awaited FDA approval of bemotrizinol (BEMT) , sunscreens are becoming increasingly more elegant in texture—like those of our European and Asian counterparts—and offer stronger, more stable broad-spectrum protection. (This is especially true for UVA rays, which cause premature skin aging and skin cancer.)

 That’s all the more reason to apply sunscreen—because despite what a lot of people still believe, melanin doesn’t make you immune to the effects of sun exposure. “People with deeper skin tones can still develop skin cancer, experience premature skin aging, and develop significant pigmentation concerns from sun exposure,” Dr. Henry says. All to say: This isn’t just about sunburns.
 The most important thing is that you find a formula that you’ll feel good about applying (and reapplying) daily. “Both chemical and mineral sunscreens can work well when they provide broad-spectrum coverage, have SPF 30 or higher, and are applied correctly,” Dr. Rodney says. Below, we gathered expert-approved, editor-tested, and Best of Beauty award-winning formulas that will give you the protection and glow that your skin deserves.

 Why it’s worth it: If your goal is a glowy, gleaming finish, La Roche-Posay's Anthelios UVAir Broad Spectrum SPF 50 delivers a radiant complexion while defending skin from UV rays. And it feels as good as it looks, with a formula that’s “lightweight and has a serum-like texture that absorbs quickly and leaves an invisible finish,” says Dr. Rodney. It uses the brand's patented Cell-Ox B3 Shield Technology, which combines four chemical filters that offer broad-spectrum protection with Senna alata leaf extract, a botanical extract known to defend the skin's top layer against sun damage. For a soothing touch, the formula also includes thermal spring water and niacinamide, while glycerin gives it its dewy finish.

 Sydney Malone Why it’s worth it: A tinted sunscreen is a hard-to-beat option for darker skin; they often contain iron oxides, which “provide additional protection against visible light, which is particularly important for patients prone to hyperpigmentation,” says Dr. Henry. (That’s because visible light, which is present even without sunlight, can also contribute to discoloration.) Isdin's Eryfotona Ageless Tinted Mineral Sunscreen SPF 50 uses an advanced titanium dioxide filter, a finely milled form of titanium dioxide that spreads more evenly across the skin (and thus delivers stronger surface protection against UVA and UVB rays) and partially shields the skin from blue light. Meanwhile, bakuchiol , a plant-derived retinoid alternative, helps gently brighten and smooth skin, while peptides support skin elasticity, smoothing the look of fine lines over time. The finish is sheer and non-greasy—and is effectively undetectable on skin.

 Frequently Asked Questions 
 What are the obstacles people with deeper skin tones face with sunscreen? 
 Definitely, white cast. For a long time, sunscreens didn’t cater to darker tones, which made it easy to buy into the misconception that darker skin doesn't need sunscreen at all. But that’s not the case. “Even tinted formulas don’t always offer shades that suit deeper complexions and different undertones,” says Dr. Rodney. “The texture and finish matter because people are more likely to apply enough sunscreen and reapply it consistently if they like how it looks and feels.”
 While cosmetic concerns may have kept people from properly using SPF in the past, the need for a good SPF is more than just what meets the eye. “Sun exposure can worsen melasma , post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation , autoimmune conditions like lupus , and uneven skin tone, so finding a sunscreen that patients actually enjoy wearing every day is incredibly important,” says Dr. Henry.
 Which type of sunscreen is best for dark skin? 
 Mineral filters like zinc oxide or titanium dioxide have long been associated with a white cast. “These ingredients are excellent at protecting the skin, but depending on the formulation, they can leave a noticeable residue, particularly on deeper complexions,” says Dr. Henry. Chemical sunscreens offer an alternative, since they absorb into the skin and disappear. “If avoiding a white cast is a priority, I often recommend looking for chemical sunscreens containing filters that tend to blend more transparently into the skin,” Dr. Henry continues.
 But that doesn't mean that you can't use mineral formulas if you prefer. After all, mineral sunscreens are a great option for people with sensitive skin or who may suffer from more chronic forms of skin inflammation like eczema or rosacea . “Mineral sunscreens have come a long way, and many newer formulations use sophisticated pigment technology to create a much more elegant finish,” says Dr. Henry.
 Meet the experts 
 Ife J. Rodney, MD , a board-certified dermatologist and founder at Eternal Dermatology and Aesthetic Center in Fulton, Maryland

 How we test and review products 
 When Allure tests a product , our editors look at it from every angle in an effort to best serve you. We review ingredients, scrutinize brand claims, and, when necessary, examine peer-reviewed scientific and medical studies. In addition to testing each and every product that's included in each and every review, we rely on experts who shape their fields, including dermatology, cosmetic chemistry, and medicine, to help us vet the ingredients and formulas.
 For our list of the best sunscreens for dark skin, we considered each product's performance across five primary categories: product ingredients and efficacy, packaging, fragrance, texture, and product wear. Every product was determined to have excelled in each category by our editorial team, which is composed of in-house writers and editors as well as contributors—along with special consideration from board-certified dermatologists. To learn more information on our reporting and testing processes, read our complete reviews process and methodology page .
 Our staff and testers 
 A beauty product is a personal purchase. You might be searching for a face cream to address persistent dryness or a new nail product to add to your Sunday self-care routine; you may simply be browsing around for the latest launches to hit the hair market. No matter what you seek or your individual needs and concerns, Allure wants to ensure that you love anything we recommend in our stories. We believe that having a diverse team of writers and editors—in addition to the wide range of outside testers and industry experts we regularly call upon—is essential to reaching that goal.
 After all, can we really say a skin-care product is the "best" for people over 50 if the only testers we’ve solicited opinions from folks who have yet to hit 30? Can we honestly deem a high-end diffuser worthy of your hard-earned cash if it’s never been tested on curls? We’re proud that our staff spans a wide range of ages, skin tones, hair textures, genders, and backgrounds, which means that we are able to fairly assess any beauty product that comes into the beauty closet.
